extracted.intended_audience: literate general public / readers of The Spectator (early 18th-century English readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A set of short moral and social essays (The Spectator) offering prescriptive observations on patronage, education, fame, ambition, and conduct—aimed at improving readers' manners and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debts of honour to dependants should be first discharged
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependants on great men become 'a Sort of Creditors' by virtue of accepted homage and expectations; these Debts, being Debts of Honour, ought, according to the accustomed Maxim, to be first discharged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Dependants who are placed under a patron's protection acquire an informal but binding claim ('debts of honour') which patrons ought to satisfy before other obligations. The passage contrasts legitimate patronage (power + obligation) with spurious forms where patrons lack ability or obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate patron-client relationships require power and obligation on one side, merit and expectation on the other
rubrics_metrics.description: When speaking of 'Patrons' and 'Dependants' the author excludes those without power or obligation and those worthless who intrude without call; true leagues are those 'where there is Power and Obligation on the one Part, and Merit and Expectation on the other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for a proper patronage bond: patrons must be able and bound to assist; clients must have merit and reasonable expectation of advancement. Avoid relationships lacking these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not take another's time/fortune into your service without prospect of reward
rubrics_metrics.description: He who will take up another's Time and Fortune in his Service, though he has no Prospect of rewarding his Merit towards him, is as unjust in his Dealings as he who takes up Goods of a Tradesman without Intention or Ability to pay him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clients and patrons alike should avoid arrangements where service is taken without the intention or ability to recompense; such conduct is morally comparable to taking goods with no intention to pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive dependence on patronage; success is rare
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the few of the Class which I think fit to consider, there are not two in ten who succeed ... I know a Man of good Sense who put his Son to a Blacksmith, tho an Offer was made him of his being received as a Page to a Man of Quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: prefer stable, skill-based employment over long, uncertain attendance on great men; many who rely on patronage lose years without reward and sometimes their wits or lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect patrons to change after gaining station; manage your expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man who is got into a considerable Station shall immediately alter his manner of treating all his Friends ... The Great have one particular Privilege ... of being slow in receiving Impressions of Kindness, and quick in taking Offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clients should recognize that elevation commonly makes patrons aloof and touchy; continued intimacy is not to be presumed during the patron's tenure in office and sudden distancing on the patron's part is common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two ways to succeed with great people: be considerable (independent) or agreeable (conform)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are but two Ways of doing any thing with great People, and those are by making your self either considerable or agreeable: The former is not to be attained but by finding a Way to live without them, or concealing that you want them; the latter is only by falling into their Taste and Pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive options: (1) cultivate independence so you need not rely on patrons; (2) adapt to patrons' tastes to be agreeable—warning that the latter may demand servility and moral compromise unless it springs from natural humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being agreeable often requires imitation of a patron's faults and risks moral corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: To be agreeable to another, especially if he be above you, is not to be possessed of such Qualities ... as make you agreeable in respect to him. An Imitation of his Faults, or a Compliance, if not Subservience, to his Vices, must be the Measures of your Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: compliance to gain favor may entail adopting the patron's vices and thereby losing the virtues that would enable resentment of injury; clients risk forfeiting integrity and capacity for just resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patrons employ tricks to remove dependants and avoid obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be endless to recount the Tricks of turning you off from themselves to Persons who have less Power to serve you, the Art of being sorry for such an unaccountable Accident in your Behaviour, that such a one (who, perhaps, has never heard of you) opposes your Advancement; and if you have any thing more than ordinary in you, you are flattered with a Whisper ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clients should be alert to strategies used by patrons to dismiss or delay obligations: fabricated accidents, feigned regret, whispering to flatter elsewhere, and flattering explanations to keep you hopeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawing from unprofitable attendance is sometimes proper despite patrons' resentment
rubrics_metrics.description: After all this Treatment, I must still add the pleasantest Insolence of all ... that when a silly Rogue has thrown away one Part in three of his Life in unprofitable Attendance, it is taken wonderfully ill that he withdraws, and is resolved to employ the rest for himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral justification: clients who cease servile attendance to pursue their own welfare may be harshly judged, but withdrawal can be reasonable and necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education polishes and reveals latent virtues in the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: I consider an Human Soul without Education like Marble in the Quarry ... Education, after the same manner, when it works upon a noble Mind, draws out to View every latent Virtue and Perfection ... What Sculpture is to a Block of Marble, Education is to a Human Soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epistemic/practical: proper education disinterrs hidden capacities; the metaphor encourages investment in instruction to bring out courage, wisdom, patience, etc., that otherwise remain raw or misdirected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourses of morality and reflection are primary means to improve minds
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourses of Morality, and Reflections upon human Nature, are the best Means we can make use of to improve our Minds, and gain a true Knowledge of our selves, and consequently to recover our Souls out of the Vice, Ignorance, and Prejudice, which naturally cleave to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice recommendation: engage with moral discussion and self-reflection as principal methods for personal improvement; the author sees his own essays as contributing to this aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savage 'virtues' can be cultivated by education and deserve humane treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: We see ... Courage exerting itself in Fierceness, Resolution in Obstinacy, Wisdom in Cunning ... What might not that Savage Greatness of Soul be raised to, were it rightly cultivated? And what Colour of Excuse can there be for the Contempt with which we treat this Part of our Species?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral imperative: persons described as 'savages' (here applied to enslaved Africans) show latent noble qualities that education could elevate; there is a condemnation of treating them as less than human or denying them prospects of happiness and spiritual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful in speech about merchants because credit is fragile
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame ... may be divided into Glory (hero), Reputation (gentleman), and Credit (tradesman). The most unhappy of all Men ... is the Trader. Credit is undone in Whispers ... How little does a giddy Prater imagine, that an idle Phrase to the Disfavour of a Merchant may be as pernicious ... as the Forgery of a Deed to bar an Inheritance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral norm: refrain from careless or malicious talk about traders; a merchant's livelihood and the public good depend on credit, which gossip can destroy. In disputes with merchants, take matters to court rather than diffuse calumny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct ambition toward virtue and 'act your part' well
rubrics_metrics.description: There are but few Men, who are not ambitious ... All Superiority ... may be reduced to Quality of Fortune, Body, or Mind ... As Virtue is the most reasonable and genuine Source of Honour ... Epictetus: We are here, says he, as in a Theatre, where every one has a Part allotted to him. The great Duty ... is to act his Part in Perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guidance: channel ambition into moral improvement (quality of mind) rather than mere external rank; excel in the role Providence has assigned rather than obsessing over titles or stations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles and honours are often empty; true worth is virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles at such a time look rather like Insults and Mockery than Respect ... Honours are in this World under no Regulation; true Quality is neglected, Virtue is oppressed, and Vice triumphant ... The last Day will rectify this Disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral counsel: do not be fooled by external honours—focus on internal virtue which endures beyond worldly ranks; expect ultimate moral reckoning, not social flattering, to set things right.
